passage:
Come, sit, Vaibhav. It's Yamini Aunty. I saw you on the terrace yesterday, just staring. Since your Dada died you've barely said a word, haven't you?
Let me tell you about my Nani. I was fifteen when she went, and for two days I felt nothing at all. I poured tea for the guests like a machine. Then, in maths class, the smell of a pencil box made me sob so hard I had to leave.
It comes in waves, beta, and never on time. My aunts made me sit with them at the prayers and tell stories about her. I laughed once, then cried harder, and both were allowed.
You needn't hurry any of it. Tell me one thing about your Dada. Just one.

qa.q: What made Yamini sob in maths class?
qa.a: The smell of a pencil box made her sob so hard she had to leave.

qa.q: What did Yamini feel during the first two days after her Nani died?
qa.a: She felt nothing at all: she was numb and poured tea for the guests like a machine.

qa.q: What could Vaibhav do while coping with the loss of his Dada?
qa.a: He can talk about his Dada, join the family prayers and let himself feel whatever comes, without hurrying.

qa.q: How might Yamini's aunts have felt making her sit with them at the prayers?
qa.a: They probably wanted to keep her close in the family's grief and help her remember her Nani, so her laughing and crying showed them she was letting it out.

grounding: An elder recalls her own numbness and sudden weeping after a grandparent's death, showing grief in waves, rituals and talking about the loved one.

passage:
Dolma, I know your classmate's funeral was last week. Sit down. I'm Sahil Uncle to you, but at sixteen I lost a classmate too. Ravi died in a road accident on a Friday.
For weeks I was shaken. I stopped taking the bus alone, and at night I lay awake thinking, if it could happen to him, it could happen to me. I had never thought about dying before.
What helped was company. I stayed at friends' houses, and I finally told our counsellor I couldn't sleep. In spring we planted a neem tree by the school gate with his name on a small stone. It didn't take the fear away, but it gave the fear somewhere to go.

qa.q: What did Ravi's classmates plant by the school gate?
qa.a: They planted a neem tree with his name on a small stone.

qa.q: What was Sahil afraid of after Ravi died?
qa.a: He was afraid the same could happen to him; he had never thought about dying before and was badly shaken.

qa.q: What could Dolma do now that she is shaken by her classmate's death?
qa.a: She can stay in company, talk to a counsellor if the fear lingers, and honour her classmate with a small act.

qa.q: Why might Sahil's story matter to Dolma?
qa.a: It shows a grown man who once felt the same fear and found ways through, so her own shakenness may feel less strange.

grounding: An elder recalls being shaken and fearing his own mortality after a classmate's accidental death, and what helped: company, a counsellor and a small memorial.

Counsellor's note, Wednesday. Harsha came in during a free period and said dinners at home are silent. Harsha's father has barely spoken since Harsha's Dadi died in January. He sits by the window most evenings and doesn't ask about school. Harsha said, "I lost her too, and now it's like I've lost him."
We talked about naming a need. Harsha decided to ask their father for one question about the day, and to call Bua, who visits on Sundays.
I explained that a parent's absence during mourning is grief, not a lack of love. I will check in with Harsha next week.
Gargi, school counsellor

qa.q: When did Harsha's Dadi die?
qa.a: Harsha's Dadi died in January.

qa.q: What is Harsha feeling, and what is the evidence?
qa.a: Harsha feels doubly alone: the silent dinners and the words 'I lost her too, and now it's like I've lost him' show it.

qa.q: What steps did Harsha choose to take?
qa.a: Harsha will ask the father for one question about the day and call Bua, who visits on Sundays.

qa.q: How might Harsha's father see his own silence?
qa.a: He is probably overwhelmed by mourning and unaware of how much Harsha needs him, which fits what Gargi explained about grief and love.

grounding: A parent lost in mourning seems absent; the teen feels doubly alone, names a need, reaches for another adult and learns the absence is grief.

passage:
I'm Nilesh. Moti, our dog, died on a Sunday in June, when I was fourteen. He had been slow for a week, then he just wasn't there. At school a boy said, "It's just a dog, get another one." I didn't argue. My chest felt like a tight fist.
I wondered if I was being silly. But I had fed him every morning since I was six, and he waited at the gate every afternoon. That isn't nothing.
My cousin Tarun didn't give advice. He asked, "Where did Moti like to sleep?" That night we put his blanket and collar in a small box, lit a diya and set it under the mango tree. I cried properly for the first time. It hurt because it was love.

qa.q: Where did Nilesh and Tarun set the diya?
qa.a: They set it under the mango tree.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh wonder if he was being silly, and what changed his mind?
qa.a: The boy's remark made him doubt himself, but remembering that he fed Moti every morning and Moti waited at the gate showed him the love was real.

qa.q: What can someone do when others brush off the loss of a pet?
qa.a: They can mark the loss with a small ritual, like the box, blanket and diya, and stay with people who take it seriously.

qa.q: How is Tarun's response different from the boy's?
qa.a: The boy dismissed Moti as 'just a dog', while Tarun asked where Moti liked to sleep and helped with a ritual, treating the loss as real.

grounding: A teen grieves a dead pet despite people saying it is just an animal, and marks the love with a small ritual.

I'm Aadhya, and I sit behind Yash in class. His father died in March. Yesterday at the school prayer Yash stood at the back with his arms folded and didn't sing. In the corridor afterwards he said, loudly, "What kind of god takes someone like that?" Then he looked around and said sorry.
Our teacher told him, "You don't need to apologise for that." The teacher said he could be angry, and that some people find comfort in prayer and some in other people, and neither is wrong.
At lunch his uncle, who prays every morning, sat next to him and they ate without talking. I can't say what Yash truly believes. He might be angry, or just tired. But he ate the whole roti.

qa.q: Where did Yash stand during the school prayer?
qa.a: He stood at the back with his arms folded.

qa.q: What might Yash be feeling, judging from what Aadhya saw?
qa.a: He may be angry at God and perhaps tired as well: he asked 'What kind of god takes someone like that?', though Aadhya admits she can't be sure.

qa.q: How could a friend support Yash?
qa.a: A friend can let him voice his anger without judging, sit with him as his uncle did, and accept that he may find comfort in faith or in people.

qa.q: How might Yash's uncle see the moment at lunch?
qa.a: The uncle may see it as a time simply to be there, sitting and eating without talking, even though he himself finds comfort in prayer.

grounding: An observer describes a bereaved classmate's anger at God, voiced aloud, and shows that faith and people are both acceptable comforts.

"You don't have to talk," Manoj said, dropping his bag on Dhruv's bed.
"I don't know what to say."
"Cool. I brought the chess set. Or we just sit."
They sat. The fan clicked. Ten minutes went by.
"Everybody keeps telling me what to do," Dhruv said at last. "Be strong. Keep busy. Eat something."
"I'm not telling you anything."
"I know. That's why it helps." Dhruv rubbed his eyes. "Today I want company but no talking. Tomorrow I might want to talk about Aaji."
"Text me which one. I'll come either way."
"Maybe chess, actually. Badly."
Manoj set out the pieces. "I'll play worse."

qa.q: What did Manoj bring with him?
qa.a: He brought the chess set.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv say Manoj's silence helps?
qa.a: Everybody else keeps telling Dhruv what to do, so Manoj not giving advice feels like relief.

qa.q: How can Dhruv get the help he needs in the coming days?
qa.a: He can tell Manoj which one he wants that day: company, space, a distraction or a chance to talk about Aaji.

qa.q: What might it be like for Manoj to sit without giving advice?
qa.a: It may feel awkward not to fix anything, yet Manoj chooses to stay and brings chess so there are options.

grounding: A friend sits with a grieving teen without advice and it helps; the teen says what he needs, whether company, quiet or distraction.

passage:
Sit, Ira. Your Aadhya Aunty will tell you why I keep this folded letter in my Gita. I was sixteen, and the night before my Dada died I quarrelled with him over something silly, a phone I wasn't allowed. I slammed the door and didn't say goodnight. In the morning he was gone.
For months I thought guilt was my punishment. Then a teacher told me guilt is what love feels like when it has nowhere to go. So I wrote Dada a letter with everything I hadn't said, including sorry, and I read it to his photo. Slowly, I forgave sixteen-year-old me.
I still carry the letter. It reminds me to say goodnight properly now.

qa.q: Where does Aadhya keep the folded letter?
qa.a: She keeps it in her Gita.

qa.q: What did Aadhya feel for months after her Dada died?
qa.a: She felt guilty and thought the guilt was her punishment for the quarrel and for not saying goodnight.

qa.q: What could Ira do with guilt about words left unsaid?
qa.a: Ira could write a letter with everything unsaid, including sorry, and forgive the past self gradually.

qa.q: How did the teacher see Aadhya's guilt?
qa.a: The teacher saw it not as punishment but as love that had nowhere to go.

grounding: An elder recalls guilt over a quarrel and a missing goodbye, reframed as love, forgiven through writing an unsent letter.

You asked why I've been so quiet, Kamal. Fair question, because Arohi is never quiet. My grandfather died three weeks ago. When I came back to school, everybody acted normal. Rhea asked if I had done the worksheet. Nobody said a word about it. Not one person. I felt invisible, as if the loss had never happened, and I wanted to shout, "Did you all forget?"
Then Mrs. Iyer, out of nowhere, said, "It must feel strange being back." And I realised maybe they were all waiting for someone else to find the right words.
Yesterday I told Rhea, "You don't have to say anything wise. Just ask me how I am." And Rhea did. It wasn't perfect, but it was something.

qa.q: What did Rhea ask Arohi on the first day back at school?
qa.a: Rhea asked if Arohi had done the worksheet.

qa.q: How did Arohi feel when nobody mentioned the loss?
qa.a: Arohi felt invisible, as if the loss had never happened, and wanted to shout, 'Did you all forget?'

qa.q: What could Arohi try with other classmates?
qa.a: Arohi can tell one or two of them what would help, such as simply being asked how Arohi is.

qa.q: Why might Rhea and the others have said nothing?
qa.a: They may not have known what to say, which is what Arohi came to realise after Mrs. Iyer spoke up.

grounding: Classmates carry on as normal and say nothing about the loss; the teen realises they may not know what to say and tells one what would help.

The school hall in Bergen was packed for the final of the five-a-side. Freya ran onto the last pass with her tongue between her teeth, the goal wide open, and kicked the ball high over the bar. The whole hall groaned, then someone laughed, then more. Her face burned and she stared at her boots.
Alejandro, the goalkeeper on the other team, jogged over. "That's the highest ball I've ever seen," he said, grinning, "and I still nearly dived." Freya snorted despite herself.
On the bus home she kept replaying it. By Monday two other people had fumbled something worse, and nobody mentioned her miss. At Tuesday practice she asked the coach to set up the same pass again.

qa.q: Where did Freya miss the goal?
qa.a: She missed in the school hall in Bergen, during the final of the five-a-side.

qa.q: What was Freya feeling right after the laughter began?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and ashamed: her face burned and she stared at her boots.

qa.q: What helped Freya move on from the miss?
qa.a: Alejandro's joke let her laugh a little, time passed, and she went back to practise the same pass again.

qa.q: How might Alejandro have seen Freya's miss?
qa.a: He saw it as a funny, harmless moment, so he joked kindly with her instead of laughing at her.

grounding: A teen fails in front of everyone and is laughed at; shame fades faster than expected, she laughs and tries again.

"Are you awake?" Rukmini whispered from the other bed.
"Yes." Kamal pulled the blanket up. "I keep seeing it. Me, on the stage, forgetting the whole poem. Everyone staring."
"That was Thursday."
"I know. It plays every night. Why does my brain do this?"
"Tell me exactly what happened."
"I forgot line four. I just stood there. Then Mr. Sane prompted me and I finished."
"You finished," said Rukmini. "So what would you do differently?"
"Learn the poem in chunks. And not look at the front row."
"There. That's data, not a verdict. Want to practise tomorrow?"
Kamal laughed softly. "Okay."

qa.q: Which line did Kamal forget?
qa.a: Kamal forgot line four.

qa.q: How does Kamal feel about the memory of the poem at night?
qa.a: Kamal feels ashamed and embarrassed, replaying every night the moment of forgetting the poem on stage while everyone stared.

qa.q: How can Kamal treat the memory as data instead of a verdict?
qa.a: Kamal can work out what went wrong, such as learning the poem in chunks and not looking at the front row, and practise, instead of using it to judge Kamal's worth.

qa.q: How does Rukmini see the moment on stage?
qa.a: Rukmini sees a slip that Kamal recovered from, since Kamal finished the poem after a prompt, and worth learning from rather than agonising over.

grounding: Kamal replays a public failure at night and cringes; talking to Rukmini shrinks it and turns it into data for practice.
